issues.legal_issue: A person already occupying property as a tenant cannot use part performance to resist eviction unless the requirements for that protection are established, including a change in the character of possession and performance or willingness to perform the contract.
material_facts: The occupant entered possession as a tenant before the alleged agreement to sell was made.
A civil court found that an agreement to sell existed but dismissed the occupant’s suit for specific performance and found that the occupant had not disowned the character of tenant.

The occupant did not prove that the parties had changed the basis of possession from tenancy to possession under the agreement, or that an independent act in furtherance of the agreement had occurred.
The subsequent purchaser was found to have purchased for consideration without notice of the agreement or any part performance.
The eviction proceeding was based on the landlord-tenant relationship.
issues.conclusion: The occupant could not rely on part performance to resist eviction, and the eviction order was maintained. A bar of limitation alone would not defeat the defence if all other requirements for part-performance protection were satisfied.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires possession taken or continued in part performance, an act in furtherance of the contract where the transferee was already in possession, and performance or willingness to perform the transferee’s obligations; the protection is unavailable against a transferee for consideration without notice. A person already in possession must show something beyond mere retention of possession to establish part performance. A final dismissal of the specific-performance suit on merits is inconsistent with the claimant having performed or being willing to perform the contract. The Court relied on G.H.C. Ariff v. Jadunath Majumdar Bahadur, Bhagwandas Parsadilal v. Surajmal, Dakshinamurthi Mudaliar v. Dhanakoti Ammal, A.M.A. Sultan v. Seydu Zohra Beevi, Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai, and Shrimant Shamrao Suryavanshi v. Pralhad Bhairoba Suryavanshi; the last case does not make limitation alone a bar where the other requirements are met. Section 91 of the Indian Trust Act was also discussed in connection with the rule concerning a subsequent purchaser with notice.

rule.if: rent_eviction_case and agreement_to_sell_found and tenant_possession_preceded_contract and no_independent_act_in_furtherance and specific_performance_claim_rejected and transferee_without_notice

predicates.rent_eviction_case: The proceeding seeks eviction of an occupant on the basis of a landlord-tenant relationship.
predicates.agreement_to_sell_found: A court found that an agreement to sell the property in favour of the occupant existed.
predicates.tenant_possession_preceded_contract: The occupant was already in possession as a tenant before the alleged sale contract was made.
predicates.no_independent_act_in_furtherance: The occupant did not establish an act beyond retaining possession that showed possession had continued under the sale contract rather than the earlier tenancy.
predicates.specific_performance_claim_rejected: A court rejected the occupant’s claim for specific performance of the sale contract.
predicates.transferee_without_notice: A subsequent purchaser for consideration acquired the property without notice of the contract or its part performance.
predicates.part_performance_defence_unavailable: The occupant cannot use part performance to resist the eviction claim.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding involves an occupant who entered as a tenant before a sale contract, did not show an independent act changing the basis of possession, had a rejected specific-performance claim, and faces a purchaser without notice, the part-performance defence is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A new factual challenge to the purchaser’s ownership cannot be raised for the first time in a discretionary appeal when it was not raised below and conflicts with the appellant’s earlier position.
material_facts: The appellant argued in the Supreme Court that the respondent had not acquired ownership through a registered sale deed.
The respondent’s status as transferee under a registered sale deed had not been disputed in the courts below.
The appellant had not requested that the original sale deed be produced in those proceedings.
The new contention contradicted the position the appellant had taken in the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The new factual plea was not permitted to be raised for the first time in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A plea that is essentially factual cannot be raised for the first time in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, particularly when it contradicts the appellant’s position in the courts below.

predicates.discretionary_appeal_case: The matter is a discretionary appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.ownership_fact_not_challenged_below: The appellant did not dispute the asserted ownership fact in the courts below.
predicates.new_factual_plea_contradicts_prior_posit: The appellant raises a new factual contention that conflicts with the position taken in the courts below.
predicates.new_factual_plea_not_permitted: The new factual contention cannot be raised for the first time in the appeal.

issues.definition: In a discretionary appeal, when an ownership fact was not challenged below and a new factual contention contradicts the earlier position, the new contention is not permitted.
